sentence: It was how his once-for-all sacrifice is applied, and whether his body can be confined to bread we break.

records.means: We held the Roman, Wittenberg, and Anabaptist positions we refused to be wrong by Scripture's test, not merely different.
records.text: We held the alternatives we refused to be wrong, not merely different. The charge is that this made us too narrow, one way among every way people have ever reached for God. We will not answer it more gently than it deserves. Rome's own repeated sacrifice and its images: refused. Wittenberg's own claim that Christ's body sits in the bread: refused. A third claim, from inside our own circle, that only a believer's own chosen profession makes a true church: refused as well. Each time, the same test: does this reading hold against Scripture? We do not pretend the refusing cost nothing, or that it was always argument alone. It was not.

evidence.words: Rome's own repeated sacrifice and its images: refused. Wittenberg's own claim that Christ's body sits in the bread: refused.

sentence: Every claim was argued openly until the council itself judged what the text had yielded, and then bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly.

records.means: In 1523 six hundred people filled Zurich's Town Hall to test Zwingli's case against Scripture, and the council ruled for it, binding every priest in its territory.
records.text: The city council of Zurich did not simply permit the argument that launched our own Reformation there. It summoned it. On 29 January 1523, six hundred people met in the Town Hall. They were priests and laymen from across the canton, with delegates from the bishop of Constance. Enemies of the new preaching mocked the gathering as a "tinker's day." They said that nothing but tinkers were attending. That mockery moved a Zurich schoolmaster named Erhart Hegenwald to write an account of the day. He had sat through the whole disputation. "I was there myself and sat with them," he wrote, "heard and understood and remembered all that was said there." When the arguments were finished, the council found for our own side. It ordered every priest in the canton to preach the same way.

sentence: He said that while he studied, 'like some spark lighting upon our inmost soul, love was kindled' - love for the Word, and for the man who taught him.

records.means: Gregory's farewell oration recounts how Origen led him through a staged curriculum and kindled his love for the Word, evidencing learning as formation.
records.text: Gregory came from Neo-Caesarea, in Pontus, to study law, and met Origen at Caesarea. He stayed five years. He tells it himself: the teacher did not begin with doctrines. He began like a farmer testing soil - questioning, digging, watching what the young man's mind did under pressure. Logic first, to make thinking honest. Then the natural world, geometry, the stars - until the students' wonder was trained. Then ethics, not as rules recited but as habits formed, the teacher's own life teaching as well. Only then, theology - reading everything the philosophers and poets had said of God, with Scripture at the center. And under all of it, Gregory says, something else was happening: like a spark falling on his inmost soul, love was kindled - for the Word, and for this man who was the Word's friend. He gave up law. When he finally had to leave, he called it being driven out of paradise.

sentence: We can tell you what the letters say was there: a double monastery - a monasterium - for men and for women, a hostel for travelers on the road near Bethlehem, and a cave our people held to be the birthplace itself.

records.means: This witness holds that this was an established, post-persecution church that condemned clerical worldliness, answered it with ascetic withdrawal, and struck outsiders as strange.
records.text: In our day, Christians were not hiding in the catacombs. Our churches stood open. Our scholar wrote that the church had grown by persecution and then, under Christian emperors, had grown in wealth and shrunk in virtue. We said the empire's embrace had corrupted the church. We said it loudly - about everyone but ourselves. Our most famous letter mocks clergy who curl their hair, beg furniture from the women they visit, and get up with the sun to make social calls. It was written from inside the capital by a man who watched it happen. Our own answer to that corruption was to leave: trade the comforts of the establishment for sackcloth, a monastery beside a cave, and a Bible. In a dialogue by a writer from Gaul, a traveler says he stayed six months with our scholar. By our own evidence, an outsider would have found these strangest: noble women in rough dress, a fortune poured into a little town in Palestine, and Roman widows refusing to marry again so they could study Hebrew. Some people thought Paula had gone mad, and said so.

records.means: This witness holds that Jesus was God the Word made flesh at Bethlehem, near whose cave the community lived, and that his poverty called them to renunciation.
records.text: We held that Jesus is the Word of God made flesh. He was made flesh in the very place where we chose to live and die. We made our home in Bethlehem, near the cave we held to be his birthplace. The Lord of all things entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough. So we counted wealth, rank, and comfort as things to lay down in order to come near him. Jerome reports that Paula saw the infant in the manger with the eyes of faith. She greeted Bethlehem as the house of bread, where the Bread come down from heaven was born. To the virgin, Jesus was the Bridegroom, whose love outweighed every earthly marriage. To the scholar, he was the Word, worth a lifetime of labor to translate truly - the translation labor later called the Vulgata. We held his death to be redemption. His resurrection was the promise we staked everything on: the treasure is in heaven, and the heart can follow it there.

sentence: The good will is kindled by him, not struck by ourselves.

records.means: Cassian reports Chaeremon teaching that grace kindles desire, enables virtue and preserves it without destroying free will, and that their union exceeds human reason.
records.text: And therefore it is laid down by all the Catholic fathers who have taught perfection of heart not by empty disputes of words, but in deed and act, that the first stage in the Divine gift is for each man to be inflamed with the desire of everything that is good, but in such a way that the choice of free will is open to either side: and that the second stage in Divine grace is for the aforesaid practices of virtue to be able to be performed, but in such a way that the possibilities of the will are not destroyed: the third stage also belongs to the gifts of God, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already acquired, and in such a way that the liberty may not be surrendered and experience bondage. For the God of all must be held to work in all, so as to incite, protect, and strengthen, but not to take away the freedom of the will which He Himself has once given. If however any more subtle inference of man's argumentation and reasoning seems opposed to this interpretation, it should be avoided rather than brought forward to the destruction of the faith (for we gain not faith from understanding, but understanding from faith, as it is written: "Except ye believe, ye will not understand" ) for how God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man.

sentence: We gave the confession itself, as the household said it together, week after week.

records.text: And in Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord, Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried, descended to Hell, on the third day rose again from the dead, ascended to Heaven and sat down at the right hand of God the Almighty Father. From there He will come to judge the living and the dead. What does this mean? I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord! He redeemed me, a lost and condemned person, bought and won me from all sins, death and the authority of the Devil. It did not cost Him gold or silver, but His holy, precious blood, His innocent body--His death! sentence: We worked over the text of scripture word by word, because we believed the writings were the true treasure handed down.

records.means: This witness holds that the community knew Jesus through scripture it carefully corrected against the Greek and the Hebrew, the churches' worship, and the holy places, without any eyewitness chain.
records.text: First and above everything, we had the writings about Jesus. The whole of scripture was copied, compared, and corrected. The Gospels were revised against the Greek. The Old Testament was translated from the Hebrew, which Jerome held truest - the Hebraica veritas. We worked over the text word by word, because we believed the writings were the true treasure handed down, worth a lifetime of exactness. More than three centuries stood between us and the events. Our confidence stood on three things: the apostles' writings as received, the worship of the churches, and - unusually - the places themselves. We could walk to the cave of the birth. The land itself we treated as a kind of witness, and our founders crossed the sea to live inside it. We held the resurrection to be true on the strength of the writings we trusted enough to spend a life correcting, and on a hope strong enough that people gave away fortunes on it.

sentence: It was a Christological argument, and this was its premise: the Word had to become flesh because sin passed to all Adam's children, and only the Incarnation could save us.

records.means: Leo's 449 letter assumes, as settled premise, that original sin passed to all Adam's descendants and only the Word made flesh saves from condemnation.
records.text: Yes, we taught that original sin passed down from Adam to everyone. Our own record says so in plain words, in a letter written against a different error entirely. Writing to Constantinople against Eutyches, Leo states why the Word had to become flesh at all. The state of everyone descended from our first parents was this: original sin passed down to all. No one would have escaped condemnation if the Word had not become flesh and lived among us. Leo reaches for Paul to say it twice over. As by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by one man's obedience many will be made righteous. As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. Sin passed down from Adam, needing a second Adam to undo it. Leo states it as settled doctrine, not as one side of a live argument.

sentence: We have nothing written for you about what to do when the person you need to make peace with will not be reconciled.

records.means: Hermas teaches that a slow answer to prayer is not refusal, and one community made confession and reconciliation a precondition of shared worship.
records.text: One of us was told plainly: if your prayer is slow to be answered, that is not the same as being refused. Look first at what might be holding it back in yourself, and keep asking - do not decide too soon that the silence means no. On forgiving, in at least one of our own communities, it was not something worked out alone in your own head. Before they made their offering together, they confessed their wrongs before the assembly, and made peace with anyone they were at odds with first. We do not know how far this specific practice reached beyond that community. We should say plainly, too: we have nothing written for you about forgiving someone who will not be reconciled. Our manual says only that no one should speak to a person who wronged another, until that person repents. This practice assumed the other person was still there, in the room, able to be made right with.

sentence: It happened once, bodily, on a day.

records.means: This telling covers entry by washing, with the forced-entry charges and the lay reluctance Augustine concedes, readmission after wrongdoing, which followed no consistent rule, and three stray fragments of prayer, chalice and fast.
records.text: If you came to us from the other communion, we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient - so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked. It happened once, bodily, on a day. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose. Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong. What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated.
